subject: Anthropology
title: Out of Africa
description: A quick win: understand Out of Africa.

hook.text: Every human alive today descends from a small group that left Africa roughly 70,000 years ago. One exodus.

buildup.text: Genetic and fossil evidence supports the Out of Africa model: modern humans evolved in Africa and then spread globally.

discovery.text: They crossed into the Middle East, then reached Australia by 65,000 years ago and Europe by 45,000 years ago.

twist.text: Along the way, they met and interbred with Neanderthals and Denisovans — our migration was never a clean sweep.

climax.text: Out of Africa explains why all humans are one species. Our diversity is young; our shared ancestry is deep.

punchline.text: We all walked the same path out of Africa.

quiz.question: What does the Out of Africa model propose?
options: Humans evolved independently on each continent
Modern humans evolved in Africa and spread globally
Africa was the last continent settled

details.summary: The Out of Africa model holds that anatomically modern Homo sapiens evolved in Africa around 300,000 years ago and migrated outward beginning roughly 70,000 years ago, eventually replacing or absorbing other human populations worldwide. Genetic and fossil evidence strongly supports this model.
details.whyItMatters: Out of Africa establishes that all living humans share recent African origins, undermining racial classification by showing that human genetic diversity is greatest within Africa and that non-African populations are a subset of African diversity.
takeaways: Modern humans evolved in Africa around 300,000 years ago
Migration out of Africa began roughly 70,000 years ago
All living humans share recent common African ancestry

faq.question: Did modern humans completely replace all other human species?
faq.answer: Not completely. While modern humans largely replaced Neanderthals, Denisovans, and other archaic populations, they also interbred with them. Non-African populations carry 1 to 4 percent Neanderthal DNA and some carry Denisovan DNA, indicating absorption rather than pure replacement.

faq.question: Why did humans leave Africa?
faq.answer: Climate fluctuations, population pressure, and the human capacity for cultural adaptation likely all played roles. As populations grew and environments shifted, some groups moved into new territories.
